farraa:6-6.t: His saying: ﴿وَيَري فِرْعَوْنُ وَهَامَانَ وَجُنُودُهُمَا﴾: this is how the companions of ʿAbd Allāh read it, with the yāʾ and the nominative. The people after them read it with the nūn: ﴿وَنُرِيَ فِرْعَوْنَ وَهَامَانَ وَجُنُودَهُمَا﴾ in the accusative. Had it been read with the yāʾ and Pharaoh in the accusative, meaning ﴿ويُرِىَ اللهُ فرعون﴾ ("and that Allah should show Pharaoh"), the verb would belong to Allah; but I have not heard anyone read it so.

farraa:8-8.t: His saying: ﴿عَدُوّاً وَحَزَناً﴾: this is [the reading] of the companions of ʿAbd Allāh [Translator's note: presumably ḥuznan, as the contrast that follows implies], and the generality [read] ﴿حَزَنا﴾. It seems that al-ḥuzn is the noun — like grief and the like — and that al-ḥazan is the maṣdar (verbal noun). The two are like al-ʿudm and al-ʿadam.

farraa:9-9.t:
His saying: ﴿وَقَالَتِ ٱمْرَأَةُ فِرْعَوْنَ قُرَّةُ عَيْنٍ لِّي وَلَكَ﴾: You put ﴿قُرّةُ عَيْنٍ﴾ in the nominative by implying (هو) (he is); the like of it in the Quran is frequent, put in the nominative by an implied pronoun.
His saying: ﴿لاَ تَقْتُلُوهُ﴾: in the reading of ʿAbd Allāh: (لا تقتلوه قُرَّةُ عين لى ولك) ("Do not kill him — a comfort of the eye for me and for you"). I have mentioned this only because I heard the one called Ibn Marwān al-Suddī mention from al-Kalbī from Abū Ṣāliḥ from Ibn ʿAbbās that he said: she said (قُرَّةَ عَيْنٍ لِّي وَلَكَ لاَ) ("a comfort of the eye for me — and for you, no"), and that is a solecism (laḥn). The reading of ʿAbd Allāh strengthens you in rejecting it.
His saying: ﴿وَهُمْ لاَ يَشْعُرُونَ﴾ means the Children of Israel; that is one view. It may also be that this is the saying of Allah: and they did not perceive that Mūsā was the one who would strip them of their kingdom.

farraa:10-10.t: His saying: ﴿وَأَصْبَحَ فُؤَادُ أُمِّ مُوسَىٰ فَارِغاً﴾: it became empty for her worry, so nothing mixed with the worry over Mūsā. His saying ﴿إِن كَادَتْ لَتُبْدِي بِهِ﴾ means: [disclose] the name of Mūsā, that he was her son. That is because her breast became constricted at the saying of Pharaoh's people, "He is Pharaoh's son", so she almost disclosed [it], i.e. revealed it. In the reading of ʿAbd Allāh: ﴿إن كادت لَتُشعِرُ بِهِ﴾ ("she almost made it known"). Abū al-ʿAbbās related to us: Muḥammad related to us: al-Farrāʾ related to us, saying: Ibn Abī Yaḥyā related to me, with a chain of his, that Faḍāla ibn ʿUbayd al-Anṣārī, one of the Companions of the Prophet, upon him be peace, read (وَأَصْبَحَ فُؤَادُ أُمِّ مُوسَىٰ فَزِعاً) ("terrified"), from al-fazaʿ (terror).

farraa:11-11.t: His saying: ﴿وَقَالَتْ لأُخْتِهِ قُصِّيهِ﴾: follow his trail. ﴿فَبَصُرَتْ بِهِ عَن جُنُبٍ﴾: he says: she was on the bank of the river until she saw that Pharaoh's people had picked him up. His saying ﴿وَهُمْ لاَ يَشْعُرُونَ﴾ means: Pharaoh's people did not perceive his sister.

farraa:12-12.t: His saying: ﴿وَحَرَّمْنَا عَلَيْهِ ٱلْمَرَاضِعَ﴾: he says: We prevented him from accepting any breast except his mother's breast.

farraa:15-15.t:
His saying: ﴿وَدَخَلَ ٱلْمَدِينَةَ عَلَىٰ حِينِ غَفْلَةٍ﴾: He said (عَلَى) and did not say "he entered the city at a time of heedlessness", although you say "I entered the city when its people were heedless" and do not say "I entered it ʿalā when its people were heedless". That is because "heedlessness" sufficed in place of "time"; do you not see that you say "I entered upon heedlessness (ʿalā ghafla)" and "I came upon heedlessness"? So since (حين) was like a surplus in the speech, and the meaning is "in heedlessness", (على) was brought in for it; and had it not been there, it would be correct. Similar is the saying of Allah ﴿عَلَى فَتْرَةٍ مِنَ الرُسُلِ﴾; had it been "ʿalā ḥīni fatratin min al-rusul" it would be like this. Similar is the saying of al-ʿUjayz:
..... ومن يكن * فتى عامَ عام الماءِ فهْو كبير
(… and whoever was a youth in the year — the year of the water — is old [now].)
Thus al-ʿUqaylī recited it to me; the first "year" is surplus.
His saying: ﴿فَوَكَزَهُ مُوسَىٰ﴾ means: he punched him (lakazahu). In the reading of ʿAbd Allāh: ﴿فَنكَزهُ﴾; and wahazahu is also a dialectal form; all are the same. His saying ﴿فَقَضَىٰ عَلَيْهِ﴾ means: he killed him.
Mūsā regretted it, sought Allah's forgiveness, and He forgave him.

farraa:17-17.t: His saying: ﴿قَالَ رَبِّ بِمَآ أَنْعَمْتَ عَلَيَّ فَلَنْ أَكُونَ ظَهِيراً لِّلْمُجْرِمِينَ﴾: Ibn ʿAbbās said: he did not make an exception [i.e. say "if Allah wills"], so he was put to trial. He made (لَنْ) a statement by Mūsā. In the reading of ʿAbd Allāh: (فَلاَ تَجْعَلْنِى ظَهِيراً) ("so do not make me a supporter"). Accordingly ﴿لَنْ أَكُونَ﴾ may in this sense be a supplication from Mūsā: "O Allah, I shall never be a supporter for them", so it is a supplication. That is because the man of his own party was met by a man after he had killed the first one, and he subjected the one of Mūsā's party to forced labour. Mūsā passed by him in that state and he cried out to him — i.e. called for his help — and Mūsā said to him: ﴿إِنَّكَ لَغَوِيٌّ مُّبِينٌ﴾, i.e. I killed a man yesterday and you call me to another! He came towards the two of them, and the man of his party thought he meant [to strike] him, so he said ﴿أَتُرِيدُ أَن تَقْتُلَنِي كَمَا قَتَلْتَ نَفْساً بِٱلأَمْسِ﴾. Pharaoh had not known who killed the first Copt. So the second Copt let Mūsā's companion go from his hand and reported that Mūsā was the killer. That is the saying of Ibn ʿAbbās: he was put to trial in that it was his own companion who pointed him out.

farraa:22-22.t:
His saying: ﴿وَلَمَّا تَوَجَّهَ تِلْقَآءَ مَدْيَنَ﴾: he means: he headed for the water of Madyan. Madyan is not declined (lam tuṣraf) because it is the name of that town. The poet said:
رُهبانُ مَدْيَن لو رأوكِ تَنَزَّلُوا * والعُصْمُ من شَعَفِ العقول الفادر
(The monks of Madyan, had they seen you, would come down, and so would the white-legged ibexes from the crags of the high peaks.)
His saying: ﴿أَن يَهْدِيَنِي سَوَآءَ ٱلسَّبِيلِ﴾: the road to Madyan; he did not know its way.

farraa:23-23.t: His saying, mighty and majestic is He: ﴿وَوَجَدَ مِن دُونِهِمُ ٱمْرَأَتَينِ تَذُودَانِ﴾: they were holding back their sheep. It is not permissible to say "dhudtu al-rajul" meaning "I held the man back". Al-dhiyād is holding back of sheep only because when any of the sheep or camels wants to stray and go off and you turn it back, that is dhawd, which is holding back. In the reading of ʿAbd Allāh: (وَدُونَهُمُ امْرَأَتَانِ حَابِسَتَانِ) ("and beyond them two women holding back [their flocks]"). He asked them about their holding back, and they said: we are not strong enough to water along with the people until they drive off [their flocks]. So he went to the people of the water and asked them to give him a bucket. They said: draw water, if you are strong enough — and the bucket was carried by forty men or thereabouts. He drew water by himself alone and watered their sheep. That is the saying of one of the two girls: ﴿إنَّ خَيْرَ مَنِ اسْتَأْجَرْتَ القَوِىُّ الأَمِينُ﴾. His strength was his drawing out the bucket alone; and his trustworthiness was that one of the two girls said, "My father calls you", and he rose with her; she walked in front of him, and the wind blew her clothes and pressed them against her body, so he said to her: "Walk behind; and if I go astray, guide me." So she walked behind him; that was his trustworthiness.

farraa:27-27.t: His saying: ﴿عَلَىٰ أَن تَأْجُرَنِي ثَمَانِيَ حِجَجٍ﴾: he says: that you make my reward [for my daughter] that you tend my sheep for me for eight years. ﴿فَإِنْ أَتْمَمْتَ عَشْراً فَمِنْ عِندِكَ﴾: he says: that is voluntary. Ibn ʿAbbās mentioned that he completed the longer and better of the two terms.

farraa:28-28.t:
His saying: ﴿أَيَّمَا ٱلأَجَلَيْنِ قَضَيْتُ﴾: He placed (ما), which is one of the connectives (ṣilāt) of the conditional, with (أى). In the reading of ʿAbd Allāh: (أىَّ الأجلين مَا قَضَيْتُ فَلاَ عُدْوَانَ عَلَىَّ), and this is more frequent in the speech of the Arabs than the first.
The poet said:
وأيَّهما ما أتْبَعَنَّ فإننى * حَريصٌ على إثْرِ الذى أنَا تابعُ
(Whichever of the two I follow, I am eager on the track of the one I follow.)
Al-Kisāʾī heard a Bedouin say: "Whichever of them takes it rides on whichever of them" — meaning in a game of theirs. That is also permissible and good.

farraa:29-29.t: His saying: ﴿أَوْ جَذْوَةٍ مِّنَ ٱلنَّارِ﴾: ʿĀṣim read it (أَوْ جَذْوَةٍ) with fatḥa, and the reading [of others] is with kasra on the jīm, or [140/a] with ḍamma on it. It is like awṭaʾtuka ʿishwatan, ʿushwatan and ʿashwatan (I led you blindly), and al-raghwa, al-rughwa and al-righwa (froth). Of the same kind is rabwa, rubwa and ribwa (hillock).

farraa:32-32.t:
His saying: ﴿وَٱضْمُمْ إِلَيْكَ جَنَاحَكَ مِنَ ٱلرُّهْبِ﴾ and ﴿الرَّهَبِ﴾: the people of Medina read it ﴿الرّهَب﴾, and ʿĀṣim and al-Aʿmash (الرُّهْبِ).
His saying: ﴿فَذَانِكَ بُرْهَانَانِ﴾: the readers agree on the light nūn in ﴿ذَانِكَ﴾, but many of the Arabs say ﴿فذانّك﴾, ﴿وهذانّ﴾ qāʾimān, and ﴿واللذانِّ يأْتِيانهِا مِنْكُمْ﴾, doubling the nūn.
His saying: ﴿وَٱضْمُمْ إِلَيْكَ جَنَاحَكَ﴾: he means his staff in this place. Al-janāḥ in the other place is what lies between the lower end of the upper arm and the rufgh, which is the armpit.

farraa:34-34.t: His saying: ﴿رِدْءاً يُصَدِّقُنِي﴾ is read in the jussive and in the nominative. Whoever puts it in the nominative makes it a ṣila (qualifying clause) of al-ridʾ; whoever puts it in the jussive does so on [the basis of] the condition. Al-ridʾ is help; you say: ardaʾtu al-rajul, I helped him. The people of Medina say (رِداً يُصّدِّقْنِى) without hamza, with the jussive on [the basis of] the condition: "send him with me, [and] he will confirm me", like ﴿يَرِثُنِى وَيَرِث﴾.

farraa:38-38.t:
His saying: ﴿فَأَوْقِدْ لِي يٰهَامَانُ عَلَى ٱلطِّينِ﴾: he says: bake bricks for me — it is al-ujūr and al-ājurr. And he recited:
كأنَّ عينيه من الغُؤور * قَلْتان فى جَوف صَفاً منقور * عُولى بالطين وبالأجور *
(As if his two eyes, from their sunkenness, were two rock-pools in the hollow of a carved rock, raised up with clay and baked bricks.)

farraa:48-48.t:
His saying: ﴿قَالُواْ سِحْرَانِ تَظَاهَرَا﴾: they mean the Torah and the Quran. And it is said ﴿سَاحِران تَظَاهَرَا﴾ ("two sorcerers supporting each other"): they mean Muhammad and Mūsā, may Allah bless them both and grant them peace. ʿĀṣim and al-Aʿmash read (سِحْرانِ).
Abū al-ʿAbbās related to us, saying: Muḥammad related to us, saying: al-Farrāʾ related to us, saying: more than one person related to me from Ismāʿīl ibn Abī Khālid from Abū Razīn that he read (سِحْرانِ تَظَاهَرا).
He said: Sufyān ibn ʿUyayna said from Ḥumayd: Mujāhid said: I asked Ibn ʿAbbās, while ʿIkrima was with him, and he did not answer me. When it was the third time, ʿIkrima said: you have pressed him too much [about] (سَاحِرَان تَظَاهَرَا), and Ibn ʿAbbās did not object — or he said: had he objected to it he would have changed it. ʿIkrima used to read (سِحْرَانِ) without an alif, and he would adduce as proof His saying: ﴿قُلْ فأْتُوا بكِتابٍ مِنْ عندِ الله هُوَ أَهْدَى منهما أَتَّبِعْهُ﴾. The people of Medina and al-Ḥasan read it (سَاحِرَان تظَاهَرَا).

farraa:49-49.t: His saying: ﴿أَتَّبِعْهُ﴾ is nominative [i.e. if read attabiʿuhu], being a ṣila of "a book" because it is indefinite; and if you put it in the jussive — which is the [preferred] way — you make it the apodosis of the command.

farraa:51-51.t: His saying: ﴿وَلَقَدْ وَصَّلْنَا لَهُمُ ٱلْقَوْلَ﴾: he says: We sent down to them the Quran, one part of it following another.

farraa:53-53.t:
His saying: ﴿إنَّا كُنَّا مِن قَبْلِهِ مُسْلِمِينَ﴾: It may be asked: how did they submit (aslamū) before the Quran and before Muhammad ﷺ? That is because they used to find the description of the Prophet ﷺ in their scripture, and they believed in it; that was their submission.
And in ﴿مِن قَبْلِهِ﴾ this hāʾ is for the Prophet, upon him be peace. Had the hāʾ been an allusion to the Quran, it would be correct, because they had said: "It is the truth from our Lord"; so the hāʾ here can be for the Quran as well as for Muhammad ﷺ.

farraa:56-56.t:
His saying: ﴿إِنَّكَ لاَ تَهْدِي مَنْ أَحْبَبْتَ﴾: love here may be taken in two ways. One of them: you do not guide whom you love because of kinship.
The other way: he means: you do not guide whomever you would love to be guided — like your saying "you do not guide whom you wish" — as you see frequently in the Revelation: ﴿وَلَـٰكِنَّ ٱللَّهَ يَهْدِي مَن يَشَآءُ﴾ to guide.

farraa:57-57.t:
His saying: ﴿أَوَلَمْ نُمَكِّن لَّهُمْ حَرَماً آمِناً﴾: Quraysh said: O Muhammad, nothing prevents us [Translator's note: the source has «يا يمنعنا», evidently for «ما يمنعنا»] from believing in you and confirming you except that the Arabs are on our religion, so we fear that we will be wiped out if we believe in you. So Allah sent down ﴿أَوَلَمْ نُمَكِّن لَّهُمْ﴾ — [i.e. have We not] settled them in ﴿حَرَماً آمِناً﴾, where whoever enters it does not fear that a ḥadd punishment or retaliation will be applied to him? So how do they fear that the Arabs will deem it lawful to fight them in it?
His saying: ﴿يُجْبَىٰ إِلَيْهِ ثَمَرَاتُ كُلِّ شَيْءٍ﴾ and ﴿تُجْبَى﴾: yujbā is masculine even though "fruits" is feminine, because you have separated the two with ilayhi, as the poet said: [140/b]
إنّ امرءًا غَرَّه منكُنَّ واحدُةٌ * بعدى وَبعدك فى الدنيا لمغرور
(A man whom one of you [women] has deluded, after me and after you, in this world, is surely deluded.)
And another said:
لقد ولدَ الأُخيطلَ أُمُّ سَوْء * على قِمَع اسْتِها صُلُب وشَامُ
(An evil mother bore little al-Akhṭal, with crosses and tattoo-marks on her rump.)

farraa:58-58.t:
His saying: ﴿وَكَمْ أَهْلَكْنَا مِن قَرْيَةٍ بَطِرَتْ مَعِيشَتَهَا﴾: baṭirathā means: it was ungrateful for it and lost it. Your putting "livelihood" in the accusative is of the same kind as His saying ﴿إلاّ مَنْ سَفِهَ نَفْسَهُ﴾. The meaning, and Allah knows best, is only: its livelihood made it insolent (abṭarathā maʿīshatuhā), as you say: "your wealth made you insolent, and you were insolent over it (baṭirtahu)", and "your opinion made you foolish, and you were foolish in it (safihtahu)". "Livelihood" is mentioned because the verb originally belonged to it, and was then transferred to that to which it is annexed. Its accusative is like the accusative in His saying ﴿فإنْ طِبْنَ لَكُمْ عَنْ شَىءٍ مِنْهُ نَفْساً﴾: do you not see that "being pleased" belonged to the soul, and when you transferred it to the owner of the soul, "soul" came out in the accusative to specify the meaning of "being pleased"? Likewise ﴿ضقنا به ذَْرْعاً﴾: the meaning was only "our capacity (dharʿunā) was straitened by it".
His saying: ﴿لَمْ تُسْكَن مِّن بَعْدِهِمْ إِلاَّ قَلِيلاً﴾: its meaning is: they fell into ruin after them, and none of them was inhabited except a little, the rest being in ruin. You see the wording as though they were inhabited a little and then abandoned, but the meaning is as I have told you. Similar is: "I did not give you your dirhams except a little", meaning only: except a little of them.

farraa:59-59.t: His saying: ﴿حَتَّىٰ يَبْعَثَ فِيۤ أُمِّهَا﴾: the Mother of Towns (umm al-qurā) is Mecca. It is called the Mother of Towns only because the earth — according to what they mention — was spread out from beneath it.

farraa:66-66.t: His saying: ﴿فَهُمْ لاَ يَتَسَآءَلُونَ﴾: Someone may say: Allah said ﴿وَأَقْبَلَ بَعْضُهُمْ عَلَى بَعْضٍ يَتَسَاءَلُونَ﴾, so how did He say here ﴿فَهُمْ لاَ يَتَسَآءَلُونَ﴾? The exegesis says: the arguments were obscured for them on that day, so they fell silent; that is His saying ﴿فَهُمْ لاَ يَتَسَآءَلُونَ﴾ at that hour, and they do not speak.

farraa:67-67.t: His saying: ﴿فَعَسَىٰ أَن يَكُونَ مِنَ ٱلْمُفْلِحِينَ﴾: As for every instance of ﴿عَسَى﴾ in the Quran, it has been mentioned to us that it is binding (wājiba, i.e. certain to happen).

farraa:68-68.t: His saying: ﴿مَا كَانَ لَهُمُ ٱلْخِيَرَةُ﴾: one says al-khiyara and al-khīra [Translator's note: the two forms are not distinguished in the vowelling of the source], and al-ṭiyara and al-ṭīra. The Arabs say: "Give me the choice (al-khayra) of them" and "al-khiyara". All of that is the thing chosen, whether man, woman or beast; any of these three [forms] is sound in it.

farraa:71-71.t: His saying: ﴿إِن جَعَلَ ٱللَّهُ عَلَيْكُمُ ٱلْلَّيْلَ سَرْمَداً﴾: perpetual, with no day along with it. They say: "I left him sarmadan samdan" — an itbāʿ (rhyming echo-word).

farraa:73-73.t: His saying: ﴿جَعَلَ لَكُمُ ٱلْلَّيْلَ وَٱلنَّهَارَ لِتَسْكُنُواْ فِيهِ وَلِتَبتَغُواْ مِن فَضْلِهِ﴾: If you wish, you may make the hāʾ refer to the night specifically and imply for the seeking another hāʾ for the day; that is permissible. And if you wish, you may make the night and the day like two actions, since they are darkness and light, so the hāʾ in (فيه) refers to both of them together, as you say: "your coming and your going annoy me (yuʾdhīnī)", because they are an action, and an action's plural and dual are referred back to the singular; so that is correct.

farraa:76-76.t:
His saying: ﴿إِنَّ قَارُونَ كَانَ مِن قَوْمِ مُوسَىٰ فَبَغَىٰ عَلَيْهِمْ﴾: he was his cousin (the son of his paternal uncle). ﴿فَبَغَىٰ عَلَيْهِمْ﴾: his transgression against them was that he said: if prophethood belongs to Mūsā, and the altar and the offering that is offered are in the hand of Hārūn, then what is there for me?
His saying: ﴿وَآتَيْنَاهُ مِنَ ٱلْكُنُوزِ مَآ إِنَّ مَفَاتِحَهُ لَتَنُوءُ بِٱلْعُصْبَةِ﴾: their weighing down (nawʾ) the band is that they burden them. The band (al-ʿuṣba) here is forty men, and mafātiḥuhu are his storehouses. The meaning is: whose keys would make the band bend (la-tunīʾu), i.e. make them lean from their weight. When you bring in the bāʾ you say: tanūʾu bihim and tunīʾu bihim, as He said ﴿آتُونى أُفرِغْ عَلَيْهِ قِطْراً﴾, the meaning being: bring me molten copper (iʾtūnī bi-qiṭrin) that I may pour on it; when you drop the bāʾ you add an alif to the beginning of the verb. Similar is ﴿فَأَجَاءَهَا المَخَاضُ﴾, whose meaning is: the labour pains brought her (jāʾa bihā). One of the people of Arabic [learning] said: the meaning is "the band would be weighed down by its keys", and the verb was transferred to the keys, as the poet said:
إن سراجاً لكريم مفخره * تَحْلَى به العَيْنُ إذا ما تَجْهَرُه
(Sirāj is noble in his glory; the eye delights in him whenever it beholds him.)
— whereas it is he who is pleasing to the eye. If he heard a transmitted report for this, then it is a valid view; otherwise the man did not know the meaning. One of the Arabs recited to me:
حتى إذا ما التأمَتْ مَوَاصِلُهْ * وناء فى شقٍّ الثِّمالِ كاهِلُهْ
(Until, when his joints had knit together and his shoulders leaned over to the left side…)
He means the archer: when he took the bow and drew, he leaned over to his side; that is his leaning (nawʾ) upon it. And we hold that the Arabs' saying "mā sāʾaka wa-nāʾaka" is from that; its meaning is "mā sāʾaka wa-anāʾaka" (what grieved you and weighed you down), except that he dropped the alif because it follows sāʾaka, just as the Arabs say: "I ate food and it was wholesome and agreeable to me (hanaʾanī wa-maraʾanī)", whose meaning, when used alone, is amraʾanī; the alif was dropped from it when it was made to follow a word without an alif.
His saying: ﴿إِذْ قَالَ لَهُ قَوْمُهُ لاَ تَفْرَحْ﴾: they mentioned that it was Mūsā who said that to him, because he [Qārūn] was of his people even though he was not of his religion. He used the plural here while it was one person, like the saying of Allah ﴿الَّذِينَ قَالَ لَهُمُ الناسُ إنَّ الناسَ قَدْ جَمَعُوا لَكُمْ﴾, whereas it was only one man from Ashjaʿ. His saying ﴿الفَرِحين﴾: had it been said al-fāriḥīn, it would be correct. It is as if al-fāriḥūn are those who will rejoice in what lies ahead of them, and al-fariḥūn are those who are in it now, like al-ṭāmiʿ and al-ṭamiʿ, al-māʾit and al-mayyit, al-sālis and al-salis. One of Banū Dubayr — who are the eloquent ones of Banū Asad — recited to me:
ممكورةٌ غَرْثى الوشاحِ السَّالِسِ * تضحك عن ذى أُشُر عُضارس
(Full-limbed, her loose sash hungry [on a slender waist], she smiles revealing serrated, cool teeth.)
Al-ʿuḍāris is the cool; it is taken from al-ʿaḍras, which is cold [hail]. One says: sālis and salis.

farraa:78-78.t:
His saying: ﴿إِنَّمَآ أُوتِيتُهُ عَلَىٰ عِلْمٍ عِندِيۤ﴾: on account of a merit I have, i.e. I was worthy of it and deserving of it, since I was given it for the excellence of my knowledge. It is also said: ﴿أُوتِيتُهُ عَلَىٰ عِلْمٍ﴾, then he said ﴿عِندِيۤ﴾, i.e. so I consider it, as He said ﴿إنَّمَا أُوتِيتُهُ عَلَى عِلْمٍ بَلْ هِى فِتْنةٌ﴾.
His saying: ﴿وَلاَ يُسْأَلُ عَن ذُنُوبِهِمُ ٱلْمُجْرِمُونَ﴾: he says: the criminal will not be asked about his sin. The hāʾ and mīm are for the criminals. He says: they will be known by their marks. It is like His saying ﴿فَيَوْمَئِذٍ لاَ يُسْأَلُ عَنْ ذَنْبِهِ إِنْسٌ وَلاَ جانٌّ﴾, then He made it clear, saying: ﴿يُعْرَفُ المُجْرِمُونَ بِسيمَاهُمْ﴾.

farraa:80-80.t: His saying: ﴿وَلاَ يُلَقَّاهَآ إِلاَّ ٱلصَّابِرُونَ﴾: he says: and none is granted [the ability] to say "the reward of Allah is better for whoever believes and does righteous deeds" except the patient. Had it been "wa-lā yulaqqāhu" it would be correct, because it is speech, and speech may be treated as feminine or masculine. In the reading of ʿAbd Allāh: (بَلْ هِى آيات بيِّنات), and in our reading ﴿بَلْ هُوَ آياتٌ﴾: whoever says (هى) has in mind the verses, and whoever says (هو) has in mind the Quran. Likewise ﴿تِلْكَ مِنْ أَنْبَاءِ الغَيْبِ﴾ and ﴿ذَلِكَ مِنْ أَنْبَاءِ الغَيْبِ﴾. Similar in ordinary speech: "That (dhāka) of yours has grieved me" and "That (tilka) of yours has grieved me."

farraa:82-82.t:
His saying: ﴿وَيْكَأَنَّ ٱللَّهَ﴾: in the speech of the Arabs it is an affirmation (taqrīr), like a man's saying: "Do you not see the work of Allah?"
And he recited to me:
وَيْكأنْ مَنْ يكن له نَشَبٌ يُحـ * ـبَبْ وَمَنْ يَفْتقِر يعش عيشَ ضُرّ
(Do you not see: whoever has wealth is loved, and whoever becomes poor lives a life of hardship.)
Al-Farrāʾ said: a shaykh of the people of Basra told me, saying: I heard a Bedouin woman say to her husband: "Where is your son, woe to you?" He said: "Wayka-annahu behind the house", meaning: do you not see him behind the house? Some grammarians take the view that they are two words, meaning wayka annahu: he meant waylaka (woe to you), dropped the lām, and made (أنّ) take fatḥa by an implied verb, as though he said: "Woe to you, know that he is behind the house", implying (اعْلم) (know). But we have not found the Arabs making [verbs of] supposing and knowing govern anna while implied. That is because it is cancelled when it is between the two words or at the end of [141/b] the sentence, so when it is implied it is treated as left out. Do you not see that it is not permissible at the beginning [of speech] to say "O you, that you are standing (annaka qāʾim)", nor "O you, that you stood (an qumta)", meaning "I knew", "I know", "I thought" or "I think"? As for dropping the lām of (ويْلك) so that it becomes (ويك), the Arabs do say it because of its frequency in speech. ʿAntara said:
ولقد شفى نفسى وَأبرأ سُقمها * قولُ الفوارس وَيْكَ عَنْتَرَ أقدِم
(What healed my soul and cured its sickness was the horsemen's cry: "Woe to you, ʿAntar, charge!")
Others have said that the meaning of (وَىْ كأنَّ) is that (وَىْ) is separate from (كأنّ), as when you say to a man: "Way! Do you not see what is in front of you?" — he said "way", then began afresh with (كأنّ), meaning ﴿ْكَأَنَّ ٱللَّهَ يَبْسُطُ ٱلرِّزْقَ﴾; [way] is [an expression of] wonder, and (كأنَّ) is in the sense of supposing and knowing. This is a sound view. But the Arabs did not write it separately; had it been like this, they would have written it separately. It may be that speech with it became frequent, so it was joined to what is not part of it, just as the Arabs agreed on writing ﴿يا بْنَ أُمَّ﴾ as ﴿يابْنَؤُمَّ﴾. He said: and thus I saw it in the muṣḥaf of ʿAbd Allāh, and it is so in our copies too.
His saying: ﴿لَخَسَفَ بِنَا﴾: the reading of the generality is (لَخُسِفَ). Shayba and al-Ḥasan — as far as I know — read it (لخَسَفَ بنا). In the reading of ʿAbd Allāh it is (لانْخُسِف بِنَا), and this is evidence for whoever reads ﴿لخُسِفَ﴾.

farraa:85-85.t: His saying: ﴿إِنَّ ٱلَّذِي فَرَضَ عَلَيْكَ﴾: he says: [the One who] sent down the Quran to you ﴿لَرَادُّكَ إلَى مَعَاد﴾. They mention that Jibrīl said: O Muhammad, do you long for your birthplace and your homeland? He said: yes. He said: so he said to him what was sent down to him: ﴿نَّ ٱلَّذِي فَرَضَ عَلَيْكَ ٱلْقُرْآنَ لَرَآدُّكَ إِلَىٰ مَعَادٍ﴾, meaning to Mecca. By al-maʿād here He meant only where you were born; it is not from al-ʿawd (returning). It may also be that His saying ﴿لرادُّكَ﴾ refers to your coming to return to Mecca, conquered for you; then al-maʿād is [an expression of] wonder: ﴿إلى مَعَادٍ﴾ — what a return! — because of what He promised him of the conquest of Mecca.

farraa:86-86.t: His saying: ﴿وَمَا كُنتَ تَرْجُوۤ أَن يُلْقَىٰ إِلَيْكَ ٱلْكِتَابُ إِلاَّ رَحْمَةً مِّن رَّبِّكَ﴾: except that your Lord had mercy on you ﴿فأنزل عليك﴾; so it is a discontinuous exception (istithnāʾ munqaṭiʿ). Its meaning is: you did not hope to know the books of the ancients and their stories, reciting them to the people of Mecca, when you were not present at them and did not witness them. The evidence for that is His saying in this sūra ﴿وَمَا كُنْتَ ثَاوِياً فى أَهْلِ مَدْيَنَ تَتْلُو عليهِم آياتِنَا﴾, i.e. you recite to the people of Mecca the stories of Madyan and Mūsā, while you were not dwelling there, staying, so that you might see it and hear it. Likewise His saying ﴿وَمَا كُنْتَ بِجَانِبِ الغَرْبِىِّ﴾, and here you are reciting their stories and their affair. This is the mercy from his Lord.

farraa:88-88.t:
His saying: ﴿كُلُّ شَيْءٍ هَالِكٌ إِلاَّ وَجْهَهُ﴾: except Him.
The poet said:
أستغفرُ الله ذنباً لَسْتُ مُحْصِيهُ * رَبّ العِبَاد إليه الوَجْهُ وَالْعَمَلُ
(I ask forgiveness of Allah for sins I cannot count — the Lord of the servants, to Whom are the face and the deed.)
I.e. to Him I direct my deeds.
